title: Grapevine
name: Grapevine
metaDescription: Grapevine 1031 exchange coordination for hospitality, retail, and airport-adjacent commercial owners trading near DFW Airport and Lake Grapevine.

sections.html: Grapevine's commercial identity is unusual for a DFW suburb because tourism and hospitality carry as much weight as any office or industrial category. Between DFW International Airport on one side and Lake Grapevine on the other, an owner selling here is often trading a hotel, a Main Street retail building, or airport-adjacent land, and each of those categories has its own quirks once the 45-day identification window opens.

sections.heading: What Grapevine Sellers Actually Have to Trade
sections.html:
Grapevine's proximity to DFW Airport and its lakefront tourism draw shape a commercial mix that looks different from most surrounding suburbs. The categories that come up most often include:

  • Hotel and hospitality property near DFW Airport and Grapevine Mills
  • Historic Main Street retail buildings tied to the wine and tourism district
  • Airport-adjacent office and logistics land near SH 114 and SH 121
  • Lakefront and Lake Grapevine-adjacent commercial parcels
  • DST interests for owners exiting active hotel or hospitality operations

sections.heading: Identification Rules for a Hospitality-Heavy Trade
sections.html: An owner exiting a hotel near the airport and rolling into a passive net lease or DST replacement almost always needs the 200 percent rule, since hospitality assets and passive replacements rarely compare cleanly enough to fit a narrow three-property list. A seller trading one Main Street retail building for a similar retail parcel elsewhere in Grapevine can usually stay inside the three-property rule, since that comparison is far more direct.

sections.heading: Diligence That Hospitality and Tourism Property Demands
sections.html: Hotel income depends heavily on management quality and seasonal tourism patterns, so a buyer should review trailing occupancy and average daily rate across multiple years rather than relying on a single strong season. Historic Main Street buildings often carry facade or preservation restrictions that limit renovation, and those restrictions should be confirmed with the city before a buyer assumes full control over the building's future use. Airport-adjacent land needs the same FAA height and noise-easement review that applies anywhere near DFW Airport, since those restrictions can cap what gets built regardless of zoning. Lake Grapevine-adjacent parcels carry their own layer of review as well, since the Army Corps of Engineers manages shoreline use around the lake and any commercial development near the water's edge should be checked against those use restrictions before a buyer assumes full development rights.

sections.heading: Financing Timelines for Hotel and Tourism-District Assets
sections.html: Hotel financing is one of the slower categories to underwrite because lenders want a full operating history and a management plan before committing, and that review can take longer than the 45-day identification window allows if it starts late. A Grapevine buyer moving into hospitality should engage a lender with hotel underwriting experience as soon as a candidate property is identified, not after due diligence has already narrowed the field. Seasonal cash flow swings tied to tourism traffic around the Main Street district and the Gaylord Texan area also need to be reflected in the lender's underwriting model, since a single peak season should not be mistaken for the property's baseline performance.

sections.heading: What a Solid Grapevine Exchange Looks Like
sections.html: The investors who navigate Grapevine well are honest about whether they are actually trading in a hospitality asset, a Main Street retail building, or airport-adjacent land, since those three categories carry different diligence timelines and financing paths, and they build their identification strategy around whichever one applies rather than treating every Grapevine property the same, since a tourism-district Main Street building and a corporate office tower off SH 114 do not share a single playbook just because both sit inside the same city limits. Even within hospitality, a boutique winery tasting room and a large branded hotel near the airport carry different seasonality, staffing, and financing profiles, and treating them as one category is a common early mistake that costs an investor real time once diligence starts.

faqs.q: Why does hotel financing take longer in a Grapevine 1031 exchange?
faqs.a: Lenders typically require a full operating history and a management plan before underwriting a hotel purchase, which can take longer than a stabilized retail or office deal. Engaging a lender with hotel experience as soon as the property is identified helps avoid running out of time before the exchange deadline.

faqs.q: Do historic Main Street buildings in Grapevine have renovation restrictions?
faqs.a: Many do, tied to facade or preservation guidelines in the historic district. A buyer should confirm those restrictions with the city before assuming full control over how the building can be renovated or repurposed, since even interior work can sometimes trigger review if it affects the storefront visible from Main Street.

faqs.q: What should I check before buying land near DFW Airport in Grapevine?
faqs.a: FAA height restrictions and noise easements can limit development regardless of the property's zoning designation, so that review should happen before relying on the site's stated development potential in an offer.

faqs.q: Should I use the 200 percent rule when exiting a Grapevine hotel?
faqs.a: Often yes, especially when rolling into a passive replacement like a DST or net lease property, since hospitality assets and passive income property rarely compare cleanly enough to fit within the three-property rule's narrower structure.

faqs.q: Can 1031 Exchange Dallas confirm my Grapevine hotel sale qualifies as an exchange?
faqs.a: No. This service coordinates planning, property identification, and communication among the investor's advisors. Whether a specific transaction and property qualify is a determination made by the investor's CPA, tax attorney, and qualified intermediary.
